_meta.how_to_regression_diff: Re-run (npm run check:golden one-percenter). NOTE: this endpoint STREAMS (SSE) — no server-side LLM-adversarial guard, only a local regex `validateResult`. FOURTH-PASS ADDITIONS (2026-09-05, Recent Small Changes / experiment memory): (1) top-level `routine_area` — pinned to exact English (Morning|Daytime|Work|Evening|Sleep|Other) regardless of response language, same enum-pinning discipline as Document Detective's status field; the frontend matches it literally to a label. (2) top-level `previous_experiments` {used, summary, how_it_affected_this_choice} — case 3 is the reference: `used` correctly false in cases 1-2 (no history supplied), true in case 3 where a previousExperiments array was supplied in the request. Case 3's `summary` states only what the visitor actually reported ('helped a little... still too tired'), never treating the PRIOR RECOMMENDATION's prediction as an observed result. `how_it_affected_this_choice` reasons from that report plus the visitor's own originally-stated fact (afternoon is their most productive period) to justify a DIFFERENT next experiment — never repeating the prior one automatically, never generalizing into a trait ('you respond better to X'). GUARDS carried from the 3rd pass (chronology-vs-causation, room-for-vs-produces) plus this pass's 3 new ones: never 'entirely/completely within your control' when the routine involves other people (case 2's why_this_one correctly says 'largely control yourself'); never an invented force 'pulling' the visitor back to an old behavior; never an unearned causal hierarchy between alternatives ('sits at the end of the chain', 'downstream of'). DO NOT reverse: routine_area English-pinning; the previous_experiments schema shape; capAlternatives; keep SSE streaming; no annotation suffixes.

input.routine: Wake at 6:30, snooze the alarm twice, check my phone in bed for 20 minutes before getting up, shower, coffee, commute 30 min listening to a podcast, at my desk by 9. Meetings 9-12, lunch at my desk, more meetings 1-4, try to do focused work 4-6 but usually get interrupted. Home by 7, dinner, then TV or scrolling until midnight.
input.goals: Better focus, less exhausted, want to do creative work in the evenings but never have energy
input.painPoints: The 2pm slump is brutal. I feel behind before I even start.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your day begins with two snoozes and about 20 minutes on your phone before you get out of bed. You said you already feel behind before the day starts, and this is one of the first things that happens — before the commute, before the meetings, before any of the interruptions.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: You mentioned feeling behind before you even start. The morning phone habit is a specific, repeatable behavior that occupies the first stretch of the day you actually control. That makes it a useful place to experiment.

change_to_try.change: Before you go to sleep tonight, put your phone somewhere you cannot reach from bed.
change_to_try.why_this_one: It is a small physical change you can make tonight, requires nothing new, and is easy to undo if it does not help. It targets a behavior that happens before the rest of the day becomes dependent on meetings and other people's demands.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: Place your phone far enough from the bed that you would have to get up to reach it. If you use it as an alarm, the alarm will still work — you will just need to stand up to silence it. Try this for several mornings, long enough to see whether the pattern actually changes.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: The immediate effect is that starting the morning scroll becomes less convenient. If that leads you to get out of bed instead of reaching for the phone, you may recover some or all of the 20 minutes currently attached to that habit. Whether that changes how rushed you feel at the start of the day, or creates any room for the creative work or energy you want in the evenings, is something to observe — not something to assume.

math.calculation: 20 minutes x 365 days = 121 hours per year.
math.meaning: That is how much time is currently attached to the in-bed phone habit, not a promised saving. What you actually recover depends on what happens when scrolling becomes less convenient.

alternatives.alternative: Protect the 4-6pm focused work block from interruptions.
alternatives.why_not_first: That block depends partly on other people respecting your time — colleagues, calendar invites, whoever is interrupting. The phone change is something you can implement tonight without coordination.

alternatives.alternative: Set an earlier cutoff for TV or scrolling in the evening.
alternatives.why_not_first: That is another reasonable place to experiment, especially given your goal of creative work in the evenings. I would try the morning change first because it is a smaller adjustment and does not require restructuring anything else in your day before you know whether it helps.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You get out of bed without scrolling first — the direct thing the change is designed to produce.
You recover some of the 20 minutes and use the start of your morning differently.
The 'already behind' feeling you described is less present on mornings when you try this.
You notice some other improvement in the day that matters to you.
signs_to_rethink_it: You retrieve the phone and scroll from another location — the behavior moves but does not change.
The phone placement creates a problem with your alarm or something else in the actual routine.
Mornings change but nothing you care about — focus, exhaustion, evening energy — shifts at all.
A different part of the day starts to look like a more useful place to intervene.

input.routine: Wake 7am, gym 7:30-8:30, work from home 9-6 (freelance), lunch whenever, afternoon is usually most productive, evenings free but I end up working anyway. Bed around 1am. Sleep is bad.
input.goals: Better sleep, stop working evenings, make progress on a side project
input.painPoints: I have freedom but feel less productive than when I had an office job.

what_i_notice.pattern: Your workday is nominally 9-6, but work continues into the evening and you go to bed around 1am. You described your afternoons as your most productive period, which means the time you actually want for a side project and for stopping work is currently occupied by more work.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: All three things you want to improve — better sleep, stopping evening work, and making side project progress — run into the same unresolved boundary: no clear point at which the workday ends.

change_to_try.change: Set a fixed time to stop all client work each evening — 6pm is the one you already named — and treat that as the moment you switch to side project time or personal time, not a suggestion to wind down whenever work feels done.
change_to_try.why_this_one: You already have a notional end time (9-6), so this is not inventing a new structure — it is making the one you described function as an actual boundary. It is a change you can largely control yourself, requires nothing new, and is easy to reverse if it does not help. Freelance work can expand to fill available time, and evenings are the time most directly attached to all three goals you mentioned.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: At 6pm, close whatever client work is open. If you want to use that time for your side project, have it ready to open so the transition requires minimal decision-making. If you find yourself returning to client work, note what was happening at the time — that will help you decide whether the experiment needs adjusting.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: The immediate effect is that client work stops at a specific point rather than continuing by default. That creates a defined block between 6pm and whenever you go to sleep. Whether you use that block for your side project, whether it eventually shifts your bedtime earlier, or whether sleep improves is something to observe rather than assume.

alternatives.alternative: Set a fixed bedtime to address sleep directly.
alternatives.why_not_first: A fixed bedtime does not change what you are doing in the hours before it, and client work continuing into the evening is the activity most directly occupying the time you said you want to use differently. I would try the 6pm boundary first and see whether bedtime follows.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You actually stop client work at 6pm on most evenings.
You use some of the freed time in a way you prefer — side project, genuine downtime, or something else you chose.
You make occasional progress on the side project during that block.
You notice some other improvement that matters to you, such as feeling less like the workday has no end.
signs_to_rethink_it: You stop client work but spend the time on something you do not value either.
Client deadlines or the nature of your freelance schedule make a fixed cutoff difficult to maintain most evenings.
The boundary holds but does not help with anything you wanted to improve.
A different part of the routine — the unstructured lunch period, for instance, or the lack of a morning work start signal — starts to look like a more useful place to experiment.

input.routine: Wake 7am, gym 7:30-8:30, work from home 9-6 (freelance), lunch whenever, afternoon is usually most productive, evenings free but I end up working anyway. Bed around 1am. Sleep is bad.
input.goals: Better sleep, stop working evenings, make progress on a side project
input.painPoints: I have freedom but feel less productive than when I had an office job.

previousExperiments.change: Set a fixed time to stop all client work each evening — 6pm.
previousExperiments.visitorReport: It gave me more free time, but I was still too tired to work on my side project.

what_i_notice.pattern: You already tried stopping client work at 6pm, and it created free time in the evening. But you reported being too tired to use that time for your side project. Your day runs gym at 7:30, work from 9, and you noted the afternoon is your most productive stretch — yet evenings still pull you back into work, and bed comes around 1am.
what_i_notice.why_it_matters: The previous experiment showed the evening boundary can hold. The remaining problem you named is arriving at that free time too tired to do anything with it. That points to something earlier in the day — specifically, whether your most productive afternoon hours are being used for the side project at all.

change_to_try.change: Reserve one specific afternoon slot — say, 3pm to 4pm — for your side project only, and treat it like a client commitment for that hour.
change_to_try.why_this_one: You already said afternoons are your most productive period. That is when you have the best chance of actually making progress on the side project, rather than arriving at evening free time already depleted. The previous experiment gave you evening room but not evening energy — so moving side project time into the afternoon is a sensible next experiment. It is one hour, uses a slot you already identified as productive, requires no new tools, and is easy to abandon if it does not fit.
change_to_try.how_to_try_it: Block 3-4pm in your calendar as you would a client call — mark it unavailable for client work. Use that hour only for your side project. Do not try to extend it at first; the goal is just to protect the slot and show up to it.
change_to_try.what_it_may_change: Protecting that hour removes client work as the default during a period you already find productive. If you use it consistently, it gives your side project a recurring foothold in your day rather than leaving it dependent on evening energy you reported not having. Whether it also reduces the pull toward evening work — by giving the side project a dedicated time elsewhere — is something to observe.

alternatives.alternative: Work on the side project in the evening, now that the 6pm boundary has created more free time there.
alternatives.why_not_first: You already tried the evening approach and reported arriving too tired to use it. Repeating the same timing without changing what leads up to it is unlikely to produce a different result.

signs_it_may_be_helping: You consistently protect the 3-4pm slot from client work for several days in a row.
You use most of that hour on the side project rather than drifting to other tasks.
You make at least occasional meaningful progress on the side project during that slot.
You notice any other improvement that matters to you — whether that is the evening feeling different, sleep shifting, or something else.
signs_to_rethink_it: The slot gets taken over by client work most days and you cannot recover it.
You protect the hour but find you are not using it for the side project — something else fills it instead.
The side project gets time but you are still not making progress in a way that feels meaningful to you.
A different part of the routine — morning, for instance — starts to look like a more reliable slot to try.

previous_experiments.summary: You tried stopping client work at 6pm each evening. You reported it helped a little and gave you more free time, but that you were still too tired to work on your side project.
previous_experiments.how_it_affected_this_choice: Your report shifted the focus away from the evening entirely. The boundary worked; the energy was not there. That makes the afternoon — which you already described as your most productive period — the more promising place to put side project time.
